Coding agents are now part of the daily routine. JetBrains’ 2026 State of Developer Ecosystem Report, based on a survey of nearly 29,000 developers worldwide, found that more than half of coding-agent users now use agents in over 60% of their work tasks.

Most developers say it pays off. Nearly three-quarters of those who regularly use AI for coding report higher productivity.

The same group reports a second job. Of developers who regularly use AI, 58% spend more time reviewing AI-generated code and other artifacts, and 42% spend more time correcting or rewriting them. If you’ve watched a senior engineer lose an afternoon to a sprawling agent-written pull request, none of this will surprise you.

That work rarely shows up when teams measure AI’s impact, and most don’t measure it at all. In LeadDev’s AI Impact Report 2026, only 31% of respondents said their organization measures AI’s impact, and 54% named quality control as a challenge. Developers feel faster while the rework shows up elsewhere, usually on whoever has to debug the result.

Developers are wary of handing over work that needs a deep understanding of code. JetBrains found they are less willing to delegate tasks such as debugging and code review. They have reason to be: in the AI Impact Report, 42% of respondents said engineers’ ability to debug without AI assistance has worsened, against 10% who said it improved.

How much developers trust AI depends on how long they’ve been coding. Among coding-agent users with one to two years’ experience, 60% believe AI produces better solutions than their own. Among those with 16 or more years, the figure is 47%.

So nearly half of the veterans rate AI’s work above their own. That’s humility, a warning sign, or both. The gap is what leaders should watch: the developers most likely to accept AI output have had the least time to learn what bad code looks like in your system.

Engineering leaders expect the same split. In the AI Impact Report, 73% of respondents expect AI to have a positive impact on experienced developers, while 63% expect a negative impact on junior developers.

Ownership is slipping too. Nearly half of developers (46%) say their sense of code ownership has decreased over the past year because of AI. It’s hard to feel responsible for code you didn’t write and only skimmed.

When fewer people feel they own the code, review becomes the main safeguard. LeadDev’s AI Code Review Report 2026 found that 47% of organizations rely on the coding agent to review its own work, and only 14% apply clearly defined, consistent standards for reviewing AI-generated code.

“AI has made code easier to produce. It’s also changing how developers spend their time,” says Kris Kang, chief AI strategist for Air Platform at JetBrains. “As agents take on more routine coding, developers are spending more time checking that the changes work as intended and fit the system.”

Security is holding back the next step. Among respondents who are unsure or think their company is unlikely to try fully autonomous coding agents in the next year, half cite data privacy and security as a concern. Given what agents can already touch, that’s fair.

In the AI Impact Report, 81% of respondents said AI tools or agents have write access to code repositories, and 32% have no formal policy for AI agents.

Start by counting review and rework as part of AI’s cost, alongside licenses and tokens. If 42% of your AI users are rewriting its output, a productivity survey won’t tell you whether delivery improved.

Then protect your senior engineers’ review time and put it in the plan, because right now it’s mostly invisible. Pair less experienced developers with them on agent-heavy work, so judgment builds as they use the tools.

Finally, make ownership explicit. Every change an agent produces needs a named person who can explain it and answer for it in production. Agents can write the code, and someone on your team still has to give them the context and stand behind the result.

The speedup is real for most developers. Whether it reaches your customers depends on who checks the output, and whether they have the time to do it properly.
